Daily deep-dive · Day 4

Write-Ahead Logging

How a database survives losing power mid-write: describe every change in an append-only log before touching the real data.

01The problem, in plain words

A database must keep two promises at once: a committed write survives any crash (power loss, kill -9, kernel panic), and writes are fast.

The naive approach — update each row's actual location in the data file as it changes — breaks both promises. It's slow, because rows live at scattered positions, forcing random disk I/O. And it's unsafe: if the machine dies halfway through rewriting a page, that page is left half-old, half-new — corrupted. A crash at the wrong microsecond destroys data.

Analogy: a restaurant during a chaotic dinner rush. The risky way: the waiter runs to the kitchen and rearranges the chefs' stations after every individual request. The safe way: the waiter first writes each order on the kitchen ticket rail — one line, always appended at the end — and the kitchen catches up from the tickets at its own pace. If the kitchen descends into chaos (a crash), nothing is lost: the rail holds every order in sequence, and you replay it. The ticket rail is the write-ahead log.

02The core mechanism

Keep a separate, append-only log file next to the real data files. Then follow one discipline for every change:

Describe the change as a small log record ("set balance of row 42 from 100 to 70").
Append it to the log and force it to disk (fsync — past the OS cache, onto the physical device).
Acknowledge the commit. The transaction is now durable — even though the data file hasn't been touched yet.
Update the real data files lazily, in memory first, flushed to disk whenever convenient.
the one rule A change's log record must be on durable disk before the changed data page is.

That ordering is the entire guarantee. Honor it and a crash can always be repaired from the log; violate it and you can end up with data on disk that no log record explains — unrecoverable.

The speed comes from the shape of the writes: appending to one file is sequential I/O, the fastest pattern a disk offers. WAL converts scattered random writes into one stream, and defers the random work to a background flush.

03Key terminology

Log record
One appended entry describing one change — typically which page/row, the old value, and the new value (enough to redo or undo it). Why it matters: records carry both directions of the change, which is what lets recovery both re-apply committed work and roll back uncommitted work.
LSN (log sequence number)
A monotonically increasing ID on every log record. Each data page also remembers the LSN of the last record applied to it. Why it matters: replay becomes idempotent — recovery compares LSNs and skips records a page already reflects, so replaying twice is harmless.
Commit record + fsync
A special entry marking a transaction durable. fsync forces it past the OS cache onto the physical device. The moment that flush returns, the transaction is committed. Why it matters: the commit lives in the log, not the data files. The data files can be arbitrarily stale at crash time and nothing is lost.
Checkpoint
A periodic operation: flush dirty pages to the data files, then record "everything up to LSN x is reflected on disk." Why it matters: it bounds recovery time — restart replays only from the last checkpoint, not from the beginning of history — and lets old log segments be recycled.
Redo / undo recovery (ARIES)
The restart procedure: redo re-applies committed changes that hadn't reached the data files; undo rolls back changes from transactions that never committed. Why it matters: after redo + undo the database reflects exactly the committed transactions — no lost commits, no phantom half-done work.
Group commit
Batching many transactions' commit records into a single fsync. Why it matters: the flush is the expensive step. Amortizing one flush over dozens of commits multiplies throughput — same batching lesson as Bitcoin packing transactions per block.

04Crash and recovery, step by step

Transaction commits: its records + commit marker are fsync'd to the WAL. Data pages updated only in memory.
Power dies. Memory is gone. Data files on disk are stale. The WAL is intact.
Restart — redo: scan the log from the last checkpoint, re-apply every change whose effects aren't yet in the data files (LSN comparison says which).
Restart — undo: any changes found from transactions with no commit record get rolled back using the old values in their log records.
Done: the database equals exactly the committed history. The crash cost a recovery scan, not data.

05Where it's used

SystemHow it uses the idea
PostgreSQL / MySQL (InnoDB)The canonical WAL ("WAL" / "redo log"): commit = log flush; data pages flushed lazily; also the basis of replication and point-in-time recovery.
Cassandra / RocksDBThe LSM "commit log" is a WAL: writes hit the log + memtable; if the node dies before a memtable flush, the log rebuilds it.
Filesystems (ext4, NTFS)Journaling = WAL for filesystem metadata, so a crash mid-operation doesn't corrupt the directory structure.
KafkaThe append-only log is the product — a WAL promoted from internal mechanism to the system's entire data model.
Event sourcingArchitecture pattern: store the log of changes as the source of truth and derive current state from it — WAL as a design philosophy.

06Common confusions

The commit happens at the log flush, not the data write. Data files can lag minutes behind. "Committed" means "in the durable log," nothing more — and that's enough.
WAL is not a backup. It's a short-lived recovery journal; segments are recycled once a checkpoint makes them unnecessary. (Shipped elsewhere, though, the same log powers replication and point-in-time recovery.)
Durability is only as honest as fsync. Some drives acknowledge a flush while data sits in volatile cache. If the hardware lies, the database's promise quietly breaks — a real and notorious class of data-loss bugs.
Sequential-ness is the point, not a detail. The log being append-only is what makes durability affordable. Forcing every random data write to disk directly would be correct but brutally slow.

07One-sentence summary

Append a description of every change to a sequential, fsync'd log before touching the real data — so a crash can always be repaired by replaying committed work and discarding uncommitted work.
